01.event: The people of the Galilee sent Rabbi Helbo a question about who reads from the Torah after the priest and the Levite, and he had no answer ready.
01.turn: Unable to answer, he went and asked Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha.
01.outcome: Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha gave him a ranked list of who reads next.
01.summary: The people of the Galilee sent Rabbi Helbo a question about who reads from the Torah after the priest and the Levite. He did not have the answer to hand, so he went to Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha, who told him the order of readers: appointed scholars, fit scholars, sons of leaders, synagogue heads, then anyone.
01.missing: The passage itself ends mid-sentence; the answer sits in the following segment. It is a thin inquiry-and-answer exchange rather than a full story.

02.missing: It is a bare citation of advice Elijah gave Rabbi Natan, with no event.

03.actor: A man who rented out a millstone, and his renter
03.event: A man rented out a millstone in exchange for grinding, then grew rich, bought another millstone and a donkey, and demanded rent in money.
03.turn: The renter refused to pay money, saying he would only grind as agreed.
03.outcome: The standoff stands at the renter's refusal; how it is resolved is only discussed later.
03.summary: A man rented his millstone to another, who paid for it by grinding for him. The owner later became rich and bought a new millstone and a donkey. He told the renter he no longer needed the grinding and wanted money instead, but the renter answered that he would grind as agreed and would not pay cash.
03.missing: The resolution (whether the renter must pay) is only found in the later discussion of Ravina, Rav Avira and the Sodom-conduct ruling.

04.actor: Rabbi Hiyya and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
04.event: When Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi was ill, Rabbi Hiyya visited him and found him crying.
04.turn: Rabbi Hiyya asked why he cried, citing a teaching that dying in tears is a bad sign.
04.outcome: Rabbi said he was crying for the Torah and mitzvot he would no longer be able to fulfill.
04.summary: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi fell ill and Rabbi Hiyya came to visit, finding him in tears. Hiyya asked why he was weeping, since a teaching says dying while crying is a bad sign. Rabbi answered that he was crying over the Torah and the commandments he would no longer be able to perform.

05.actor: Rav and Rabba bar bar Hana
05.event: Rabba bar bar Hana gave Rav money to buy a plot of land for him, and Rav bought it for himself.
05.turn: This seems deceitful, and Rav should have told him, but the land was among violent men who honored Rav and not Rabba bar bar Hana.
05.outcome: Rav's act stands: he feared someone else would buy the land in the meantime.
05.summary: Rabba bar bar Hana gave Rav money to buy him a field, but Rav bought it for himself. The Gemara objects that this is deceitful and that Rav should at least have informed him. It explains that the field lay among violent men who respected Rav but not Rabba bar bar Hana, and that Rav feared someone else would buy it while he was reporting back.

06.actor: A man who betrothed a minor girl, and Ravina
06.event: A man betrothed a minor girl with a bundle of vegetables in the marketplace.
06.turn: Ravina ruled that even if a father's consent is presumed, it is not presumed for a degrading betrothal.
06.outcome: No concern that the father agreed, so the betrothal is not valid.
06.summary: A man betrothed a minor girl with a bundle of vegetables in the marketplace, without her father's consent. Ravina ruled that the presumption that a father may have desired the match applies only to a dignified betrothal, not a degrading one like this.
06.missing: It is a case followed by a ruling; there is no real action beyond the betrothal itself.

07.actor: A man in Mata Mehasya and his brother
07.event: A man had a yevama fall to him for levirate marriage, and his brother wanted to disqualify her with a bill of divorce, apparently for the inheritance.
07.turn: The man offered to share the property, but the brother feared being cheated as in the Pumbedita story.
07.outcome: The man offered that the brother could divide the property from now.
07.summary: A man in Mata Mehasya had a yevama fall to him, and his brother wanted to disqualify her by giving her a divorce document. The man asked whether this was about the inheritance and offered to split it. The brother feared he would be cheated as the Pumbedita swindler did, so the man told him to divide the property right away if he liked.

08.missing: It is a legal question put to an elder with no answer or event shown.

09.event: A husband took a bundle of branches from his wife's property and fed them to his animals, and Rav Yehuda ruled on it.
09.turn: Rav Yehuda treated this as legitimate consumption of her property.
09.outcome: Rav Yehuda's ruling stands, explained by his general view on consuming forbidden produce.
09.summary: The judges of Pumbedita reported that Rav Yehuda acted in a case where a husband took branches from his wife's land and fed them to his animals. He treated it as consumption of her property, consistent with his rule that even eating forbidden produce counts as taking possession.
09.missing: The case is only sketched, and it is mostly a report of a ruling with its reasoning.

10.actor: Rav Hinnana bar Shelamiya and Rav
10.event: Rav Hinnana taught a mishna to Hiyya bar Rav in Rav's presence with a stringent wording.
10.turn: Rav rebuked him for abandoning the Rabbis and following Rabbi Meir.
10.outcome: The Gemara explains Rav Hinnana's reasoning and that the first clause follows the Rabbis, the last clause Rabbi Meir.
10.summary: Rav Hinnana bar Shelamiya was teaching a mishna to Hiyya bar Rav in front of Rav, but wording it in the stringent way. Rav asked whether he had abandoned the Rabbis to follow Rabbi Meir. The Gemara explains he had inferred the first clause from the last, which was wrong because only the last follows Rabbi Meir.
10.missing: It is mainly a correction of a teaching error, with the aftermath not shown.

11.event: He sat studying Torah in the lower marketplace of Tzippori while his cloak lay in the upper marketplace.
11.turn: One time someone came to take the cloak.
11.outcome: He found a serpent on it.
11.summary: Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat was so absorbed in Torah that he sat studying in the lower marketplace of Tzippori while his cloak lay in the upper one. One time a man came to take the cloak and found a serpent lying on it.

12.actor: Rav Nahman and the judges of Nehardea and Pumbedita
12.event: Judges in Nehardea ruled that daughters be supported from movable property, and Rav Hana bar Bizna did likewise in Pumbedita.
12.turn: Rav Nahman ordered them to reverse their rulings and threatened to take their houses.
12.summary: Cases came before the courts of Nehardea and Pumbedita, and the judges ruled that daughters be supported from their father's movable property. Rav Nahman told them to reverse their decisions or he would collect the money from their own houses.
12.missing: How the judges responded is not stated.

13.event: A tumtum in Biri was placed in a seat and operated on, his skin was torn open, and he later fathered seven children.
13.turn: Rabbi Ami used this as a challenge to Rabbi Yehuda's view that a torn tumtum is impotent.
13.outcome: The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yehuda would doubt the children were his.
13.summary: Rabbi Ami recalled a tumtum from Biri who was seated, torn open, and then fathered seven children, which seems to contradict Rabbi Yehuda's ruling. The Gemara replies that Rabbi Yehuda would say to go and check where those children came from.
13.missing: The incident is a brief reference used as an argument, not told as a story.

14.actor: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba and Rav
14.event: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba saw Rav say kiddush before Shabbat began and asked whether he had now separated from labor.
14.outcome: This is cited as proof that reciting kiddush accepts the day's restrictions.
14.summary: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba watched Rav recite kiddush before Shabbat began and asked whether he had thereby separated himself from work. Rav replied that he had.
14.missing: It is a two-line exchange cited as proof for a law, not a developed story.

15.event: A man brought him the first shearing, and in conversation said he also had a case to bring before him.
15.turn: Rabbi Yishmael refused the gift and disqualified himself as judge.
15.outcome: He seated two scholars to judge the case, and while pacing he found himself mentally arguing for the man, which made him denounce bribe-takers.
15.summary: A man brought Rabbi Yishmael bar Elisha, a priest, the first shearing of his flock. Learning that he had a lawsuit pending, Rabbi Yishmael refused the gift and said he was disqualified from judging the case. He seated two scholars to hear it, but as he came and went he caught himself thinking of arguments for the man, and concluded that those who really accept bribes must be even more biased.

16.actor: Heirs of a man who left a will, and Rav Idi bar Avin and Rav Yosef
16.event: A man instructed his heirs to give his daughter a dowry or 400 dinars of wine, and prices then moved so that money was left over.
16.turn: The question arose who gets the surplus.
16.outcome: Rav Idi bar Avin and Rav Yosef ruled the surplus goes to the male orphans.
16.summary: A man told his heirs in his will to give his daughter a dowry, and the cost of dowries then fell. Another man told them to give her four hundred dinars of wine, and the wine's price rose, leaving a surplus. In each case the rabbis ruled that the leftover amount belongs to the male heirs.
16.missing: The cases are brief hypothetical-style rulings; nothing about the people or what followed.

17.actor: The orphans of a man who died in debt
17.event: A man owing one hundred dinars died leaving land worth fifty, and the creditor repossessed it.
17.turn: The orphans paid the creditor fifty dinars to get it back, but he repossessed it again to collect the rest.
17.outcome: Abaye told them paying earlier was a mitzva, and now the creditor was repossessing lawfully.
17.summary: A man who owed a creditor one hundred dinars died, leaving a small field worth fifty. The creditor seized it, the orphans paid him fifty to redeem it, and he seized it again for the remainder of the debt. They complained to Abaye, who told them that paying their father's debt was a mitzva, but the payment had not cancelled the lien, so the creditor was within his rights.

18.event: Abaye was riding along the bank of the Sagya River while Rav Mesharshiya and the rabbis sat on the other bank and did not stand for him.
18.turn: Abaye protested that he was their primary teacher and they should stand.
18.outcome: They answered that they had not noticed him at all.
18.summary: Abaye was known to stand as soon as he saw the ear of Rav Yosef's donkey approaching. One day, riding along a river, he passed Rav Mesharshiya and other rabbis on the opposite bank who did not stand. He asked whether he was not their primary teacher, and they replied that it had never occurred to them, as they had not seen him.

19.actor: A man picking dates and a woman who asked for some
19.event: A woman asked a man picking dates to throw her two, and he asked whether she would be betrothed to him if he did.
19.turn: She answered only 'Throw, throw,' which does not accept the condition.
19.outcome: Rav Zevid ruled that such a statement is nothing and she is not betrothed.
19.summary: A man was picking dates from a tree when a woman asked him to throw her two. He asked whether she would be betrothed to him if he did, and she just said 'Throw, throw.' Rav Zevid ruled that this answer means nothing and she was not betrothed.

20.missing: It is only a brief report that Rav Aha asked Rav Ashi's students whether he had said anything, and they said he had not; nothing happens.
